cur:catacombs-sarcophagus-31553.summary: Short, curly-haired figures crowd the front in a single frieze. According to the museum label recorded on Commons, it shows the sacrifice of Isaac, the healing of the blind man, the healing of the paralytic, the multiplication of the loaves and fishes and further healings. The repeated image of the young Christ touching and restoring the sick gave the bereaved a vivid hope of resurrection.
facts: Commons dates it to about 300–330, the very beginning of the Constantinian period.
The naked figures at the right belong to the Adam and Eve scene, a frequent companion of the miracles on these sarcophagi.

cur:manuscripts-rossano-communion-cup.summary: On the facing page Christ, now at the right, offers the cup to an apostle who bends forward to drink, as the remaining disciples wait their turn in a solemn file. The Greek words above recall that he took the cup and gave thanks. Below, prophets raise their hands toward the sacrament.
facts: The diocesan museum describes the Communion of the Apostles as the one scene that occupies two pages of the codex.
The manuscript was restored in 1919 and again in 2012.

cur:manuscripts-valcavado-last-judgement.summary: At the top, Christ sits enthroned in a starry medallion between two flying angels; beneath him, in three crowded registers, the apostles and the elect sit on thrones with open books, judging and being judged 'according to their works'.
facts: The Valcavado Beatus was written and illuminated in 970 by the monk Oveco for Abbot Sempronius of Valcavado, in the reign of Ramiro III of León; it has 230 surviving leaves and 87 miniatures.
After the expulsion of the Jesuits under Charles III, the manuscript passed from their college of San Ambrosio in Valladolid to the University of Valladolid.

Q87480871.summary: A small, glowing orange Christ hangs on the cross beneath a yellow halo, flanked by pink angels, while dark, almost shapeless women gather below under a red-violet sky streaked with green. Painted when Denis was only eighteen or nineteen, it sacrifices realistic description for flat, intense colour meant to carry spiritual feeling directly. Denis, a devout Catholic, wanted to create 'imperishable icons' for modern times.
facts: It was painted in the same year as Gauguin's Yellow Christ, whose bold Synthetist colour deeply influenced the young Denis and his Nabis circle.
In 1890 Denis wrote the famous dictum that a painting, before being a warhorse or a nude, is essentially a flat surface covered with colours arranged in a certain order.
The panel measures only about 24 by 19 cm; it entered the Cleveland Museum of Art in 2020 as a gift from the Nancy F. and Joseph P. Keithley Collection.
